strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely interesting and underexplored application: learning to generate link topologies for directional-antenna ad hoc networks, imitating an expensive greedy combinatorial algorithm — a sensible amortization framing.

The proposed Cross-Attentive Modulation (CAM) tokens are a plausible, lightweight architectural idea (registers-informed cross-attention plus FiLM-style modulation) motivated by a real weakness of graph transformers (capturing global structure), and are cleanly described with equations and an architecture figure.

The partial-diffusion scheme for temporal topology evolution (Sec. 4.3), which uses the previous topology as a starting state and scales the number of diffusion steps with node movement, is an elegant and natural extension of the diffusion framework.

The paper is honest that a lightweight post-processing/correction algorithm (Alg. 2) is needed, and includes constraint-adherence and loss-term ablations (Tables 1 and 3), which support the value of the added losses (e.g., parity adherence jumps from 67.07% to 98.65%).
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is too thin to support the central claims. There is only one baseline (a 'standard GT' DDPM); no comparison against the greedy algorithm itself (quality vs. runtime trade-off, which is the core motivation), no comparison with prior DDPM-based topology generation (e.g., ref. [18]), and no comparison with simpler non-generative link-prediction baselines.

The claimed contribution of CAM tokens is not isolated: Table 1 confounds CAM tokens with handcrafted features and losses ('NetDiff' vs 'NetDiff (no features)' vs 'Standard GT'), so it is impossible to determine how much of the improvement is attributable to the headline architectural novelty versus the loss engineering.

The network evolution mechanism (Sec. 4.3), presented as a main contribution, is never evaluated empirically — there are no experiments on mobility scenarios, stability of topology over time, or quality of updated graphs. Its claims rest entirely on plausibility arguments.

Scalability claims (graph transformers scale better than the O(m^2) greedy algorithm) are not substantiated: experiments use only 16-node graphs, with an informal remark that 32-node results 'seemed similar', and the authors state a full 32-node test set could not be generated. No node-count scaling curve is provided.
The evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no variance, confidence intervals, or number of runs; metrics such as 'Connected 99.13%' vs '98.12%' may not be meaningful without uncertainty estimates.

Several methodological details are underspecified, undermining reproducibility: the scalar transition matrix m is only vaguely 'correlated with the true distribution of the dataset links'; dataset construction, size, and topology-generation parameters are not described; no code or data is released; hyperparameters are given only as a learning-rate range.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track submission: multiple typos ('Graph Transfomer', 'diffision', 'apropros', 'proporition', 'computionally'), vague phrasing ('Without entering into technical details'), and a results section that is mostly qualitative narration around small tables.

Generated graphs have substantially more links than the target (49.74 vs 43.90) and nearly double the saturated antennas (16.19% vs 9.74%), and average link length is notably higher (1.04 vs 0.85) — the 'realistic and close to original graphs' claim is only partially supported.

strengths: The application domain is interesting and relatively underexplored: applying discrete graph diffusion models to directional-antenna ad hoc network topology generation is a plausible and practical use of generative graph models, and the paper motivates it clearly (avoiding heavy combinatorial search and enabling topology updates under mobility).

The paper is honest that generated graphs require post-processing (Algorithm 2) rather than claiming raw generations are deployment-ready, and it provides a concrete correction algorithm with reported execution time (~250 ms).

There are some useful ablations: Table 1 separates the effect of handcrafted features and CAM tokens versus a standard graph transformer, and Table 3 isolates the contribution of the auxiliary losses (e.g., parity adherence improves from 67.07% to 98.65%).

The problem formulation is mostly well specified: the parity labeling, antenna-sector constraints, and the greedy teacher algorithm (Algorithm 1) give the reader a clear picture of what the generator is imitating.
weaknesses: The temporal/evolution component (Section 4.3) is a stated core contribution ('partial diffusion' for network updates under node mobility) but is never evaluated. There are no experiments on moving nodes, no metrics on topology stability, signaling overhead, or quality of evolved topologies. Claiming this module 'provides a robust mechanism' in the conclusion is unsupported.

The central scalability argument is asserted, not demonstrated. The paper claims O(n^2) transformers scale much better than the O(m^2) greedy algorithm, but experiments cover only 16 nodes (with an unquantified anecdote about 32 nodes: 'it seemed to display results similar'), and the authors admit they 'could not generate a full dataset and test set of 32-node-sets'. For a paper whose main motivation is escaping computational hardness, this is a serious evidential gap.

The key baseline is missing: the paper never compares generated topologies against the output of the greedy teacher algorithm itself (Algorithm 1), neither in quality nor runtime, on the same instances. Without this, claims like 'alleviated the computational burden' and 'operational' cannot be verified; throughput comparisons in Table 2 are against dataset targets only.

The CAM token ablation is confounded: Table 1 compares NetDiff, NetDiff (no features), and Standard GT, so the individual contribution of CAM tokens versus the added features/losses cannot be disentangled for most metrics. Since CAM tokens are presented as the main architectural novelty, a dedicated ablation is needed.

No comparison against existing graph diffusion baselines (e.g., DIGRESS [13], which the method builds on) or other generative approaches on any standard or adapted benchmark, making it hard to judge whether the gains are specific to CAM tokens or simply reflect task-specific features and losses.

Several quantities and experimental details are under-specified or unclear: the dataset construction (how many training graphs, what node distributions), the units and meaning of 'Average link length' (1.04 vs target 0.85 seems like a large discrepancy that is not discussed), 'Length' as 'proportion of links that respect the maximal«s possible range' (typo, unclear metric), and how the transition scalar m is set. No variance, confidence intervals, or number of runs are reported for any table.

The novelty is modest and positioned without sufficient differentiation: CAM tokens are a combination of register tokens [29], cross-attention, and FiLM-style modulation [27][28]; the diffusion setup follows DiGress [13] closely; the auxiliary losses are straightforward. The paper does not analyze when or why CAM tokens help (no attention statistics, no probing of global property capture), despite motivating them via GNN struggles with global structure.

Presentation issues undermine polish and precision: multiple typos ('Graph Transfomer', 'diffision', 'proporition', 'havenot', 'Langevinesque'), inconsistent notation (V = {v1, v2v..., vn}, Edges denoted both E and E^t with conflicting meanings between Section 3.2 and 4.3), and equations (6)-(7) whose dimensional consistency is not explained.

There is no limitations section and no discussion of reproducibility: no code or data release is mentioned, no dataset statistics, and hyperparameters are given only as a range ('learning rates between 1e-4 and 1e-7').

Claims such as 'unmatched performance' for directional-antenna networks in the abstract, and 'efficient and scalable solution for wireless network design' in the conclusion, are marketing-level statements not backed by the contained evaluation.

strengths: Interesting and well-motivated application domain: learning to generate link topologies for ad hoc networks with directional antennas is a genuinely underexplored problem where deep graph generation could plausibly replace expensive combinatorial/greedy optimization, and the paper situates itself well against prior graph DDPM work (e.g., DIGRESS) and network-focused GNN literature.

The proposed components are sensible and clearly described: CAM tokens (cross-attentive modulation registers for global graph-level conditioning) are a reasonably novel architectural idea with a plausible mechanism, and the auxiliary losses (sector, cosine, parity) are concretely defined and tailored to the physical constraints.

The temporal evolution mechanism based on partial diffusion with a movement-proportional number of steps is an elegant and lightweight way to reuse the diffusion framework for topology maintenance under mobility — a practically important concern that most graph generation papers ignore.

Empirical results show consistent gains over a standard graph transformer DDPM baseline across constraint-adherence metrics (Tables 1-3), and the loss ablation (Table 3) demonstrates that the parity loss in particular is essential (98.65% vs 67.07%).
The paper is honest that generated graphs require a post-processing/correction step, and Algorithm 2 makes this operational pipeline explicit.
weaknesses: The temporal evolution algorithm (Section 4.3) — one of the four claimed contributions — receives no empirical evaluation whatsoever. There are no experiments on node mobility, no measurement of topology churn/stability over time, and no evidence that the partial diffusion update produces stable or valid evolving topologies. This is a major gap between claims and evidence.

The evaluation scale and scope are narrow: only 16-node sets (32-node tested informally with 'similar results' but no numbers), no comparison against the greedy baseline algorithm (Algorithm 1) that the model is trained to imitate in terms of both quality and runtime, and no comparison with other graph generators (e.g., [17], [18], or non-diffusion baselines). The claim of 'alleviating the computational burden' of combinatorial methods is never quantified against such methods.

The dataset is never described: how many samples, how generated, what distribution of node placements, whether it is public. This severely limits reproducibility, and there is no mention of code release. Hyperparameter reporting is minimal (learning rate 'between 1e-4 and 1e-7', 10 transformer blocks), and no variance/std or significance testing accompanies any of the reported percentages.

The ablation in Table 1 conflates contributions: it compares NetDiff vs NetDiff (no features) vs Standard GT, but does not isolate CAM tokens from the handcrafted features and loss terms, so the specific benefit of the claimed-novel CAM mechanism cannot be cleanly attributed. The 'Standard GT' row also appears to include the loss terms, making the architectural comparison ambiguous.

Standard graph generation quality metrics (e.g., MMD of degree/clustering/orbit distributions) are absent; evaluation relies on a handful of constraint percentages and a few scalar properties. The claim that generated links are 'realistic' and structurally similar to the dataset is supported only anecdotally (Figure 1) and by sparse statistics.

Several central claims are overstated relative to evidence: 'greatly outperforms a graph transformer DDPM' rests on one baseline and small margins on some metrics; 'model is agnostic to the number of nodes' is asserted from an informal 32-node test explicitly acknowledged as incomplete ('For technical reasons, we could not generate a full dataset and test set of 32-node-sets').

Presentation issues undermine rigor: multiple typos ('diffision', 'proporition', 'Transfomer', 'viable'), an undefined/unvalidated scalar noise 'transition matrix' m, notation inconsistencies (e.g., edge set written as {e_{1,1},...,e_{n,n}}), and no limitations section discussing scale limits, dataset dependence on the specific greedy teacher, or generalization to other network regimes.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated, practically important problem: real-time generation of constraint-compliant link topologies with transmit/receive parity for mobile ad hoc networks with directional antennas, where combinatorial solvers are too slow.

ACAM tokens are a genuinely interesting architectural idea: detached global tokens that aggregate graph information via unsoftmaxed (absolute) cross-attention and inject it back through FiLM modulation, motivated by the need to track graph-level cardinalities (edge counts, sector occupancy). The CAM vs. ACAM ablation (Tables 1, 3) supports the claimed benefit.

Partial diffusion for topology evolution under mobility (starting the reverse process from the previous topology at a noise level proportional to node displacement) is a practical and elegant contribution, with reasonable evidence of improved continuity (21-41% more similar topologies) and 3.3-5x speedup.
The ablation of auxiliary loss terms (Table 4) is convincing, particularly the parity loss lifting parity satisfaction from 62% to ~98.6%.

The paper is generally honest about limitations: it acknowledges heuristic fallback in data generation, post-processing correction (Alg. 2), reduced performance on 32-node networks, and that 40+ node networks are out of scope.
Appendices provide reasonable implementation detail: data generation (Alg. 1), the throughput/interference model, and the topology correction procedure.
weaknesses: Evaluation breadth is limited: experiments are almost entirely on 16-node networks (with a single small-scale 32-node experiment), on one proprietary deployment distribution. No standard graph-generation benchmarks are used to test whether ACAM tokens generalize beyond this narrow regime, which weakens the claim that they are a broadly useful architectural contribution.

Reproducibility is weak: no code or data release is mentioned, training data generation relies on proprietary antenna radiation patterns and propagation models explicitly declared out of scope (App. 8), and the similarity metric used for the '21%/41% more similar' claims is never defined. Others cannot reliably build on or verify the results.

Baselines are relatively weak and incomplete. GraphVAE and a generic DDPM-GT are compared, but TopoFormer (Marcoccia et al., 2025), which the authors themselves identify as tackling 'a similar problem to ours', is not compared against. There is also no quantitative comparison against the combinatorial/reference solver at inference time (the constant-runtime claim is asserted but the accuracy-vs-runtime trade-off against the exact solver is not tabulated).

Several central claims are asserted rather than substantiated: that unsoftmaxed attention enables 'counting' (no analysis or probing experiment), that ACAM advantages grow with model capacity (stated only as an unquantified observation, 'additional experiments not displayed'), and that NetDiff reaches 'over 95% of target performance' (only one throughput figure at 32 nodes approaches 95%).

The factorization p(S,E|G^t) = p(S|G^t) x p(E|G^t) in Eq. (2) assumes conditional independence between parity and edges at each denoising step, which appears in tension with the paper's core motivation that topology-parity interdependence is exactly what needs joint modeling; the discrepancy is not analyzed.

Statistical rigor is thin: error bars are reported for some metrics but their provenance (number of runs, seeds, test set size) is unstated; several key differences are small (e.g., connectedness 98.68 vs 98.68, parity 98.63 vs 98.64) and unlikely to be significant. Many important numbers appear only in prose without uncertainty.

There is ambiguity about what the reported numbers include: results are claimed 'without any post-processing' yet a correction algorithm is applied 'to ensure that the networks are valid', and the relationship between Table 1-3 results and post-processed results is unclear. Hard-constraint satisfaction figures (~98.5%) may partly reflect the post-processing routine rather than the model.

Rotation invariance is dismissed by appeal to a global fleet direction, and edge angle features are defined relative to a horizontal axis; this design choice limits applicability and is justified only informally. The noise schedule description (Eq. 5) is also hard to follow as written.

The paper is borderline in scope for ICML's main track: it is a solid applied/architectural contribution, but the evaluation and theoretical grounding do not clearly establish the method as advancing graph-generation understanding beyond this specific domain.

strengths: The application problem (real-time topology generation for directional ad hoc networks with parity, sector, and interference constraints) is well motivated, practical, and not commonly addressed in the graph generation literature.

Partial diffusion for network reconfiguration under mobility is an appealing, practical idea that extends the diffusion framework beyond one-shot generation, with a sensible mechanism (starting at a diffusion time proportional to normalized node displacement).

The paper includes useful ablations: the loss-term study (Table 4) convincingly shows the parity and sector losses are necessary, and Tables 1/3 separate the contributions of domain features, CAM, and ACAM tokens.
The overall writing is accessible and the pipeline (data generation, diffusion formulation, correction algorithm in App. 10) is described end to end.
An impact statement is provided and discusses plausible misuse risks and mitigations.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is inadequate for a main-track paper. The dataset is proprietary ('realistic deployments of manned aircraft'), the exact simulation parameters are explicitly omitted as proprietary (App. 8), and no code release is mentioned. Since the entire contribution is validated only on this in-house simulator and dataset, others cannot verify or build on the results.

The central architectural claim—that ACAM tokens improve 'global coherence' and enable 'counting'—is not rigorously supported. The unsoftmaxed cross-attention is motivated only by intuition, with no theoretical analysis, no study of whether the token representations actually encode cardinalities, and no ablation of the similarity choice (cosine vs. scaled dot product). Critically, Table 3 lacks the most informative baseline: standard virtual nodes/registers (Devlin et al.; Darcet et al.) or DiGress-style statistical feature conditioning, so the benefit of the 'novel' ACAM mechanism over known global-token techniques is unquantified.

Improvements over the strengthened DDPM-GT baseline are small and reported without significance testing in key comparisons (e.g., throughput 3.35→3.52, saturation 13.6→12.1 in Table 1; saturation 7.98→7.05 in Table 3). With single-seed training (fixed seed 123) and no error bars on most tables, these margins may not be meaningful.

The role of post-processing is confusing and potentially inflates results. Section 5.1 states results are 'obtained without any post-processing', yet the following paragraph says a correction routine (App. 10) is applied 'to ensure that the networks are valid and robust'. It is unclear which reported numbers include Algorithm 2, and the throughput comparison in Table 2 may partially reflect hand-crafted repair rather than the learned model.

The most relevant competitor, TopoFormer (Marcoccia et al., 2025), which 'tackles a similar problem', is dismissed in one sentence without empirical comparison, on the grounds that it does not jointly predict parity. A parity post-assignment baseline for TopoFormer, or at least an adapted variant, is needed to substantiate the claimed advantage of joint generation.

The partial diffusion method is close to existing noise-and-denoise conditioning ideas (e.g., SDEdit-style partial noising) which are neither cited nor compared against; the claim that 'edge variations closely match intermediate diffusion states' is asserted 'empirically' with no supporting figure or quantification.

Evaluation scope is narrow: 16 nodes for main results, 32 nodes only via a separate retrained model (App. 9), and 40+ nodes explicitly out of scope. Claims of 'constant inference time' and scalability advantages over combinatorial methods are therefore only weakly demonstrated.

Presentation issues undermine confidence: several important experiments are described but 'not displayed for clarity'; Eq. (5)'s noise schedule is under-specified (the role of the one-dimensional m is opaque); Eq. (16) is malformed; and there are numerous grammatical errors (e.g., 'which allows for expressive behavior—enforcing globally', 'more effective with when using'). No limitations section is provided.

The training data generation mixes a quasi-exhaustive search with a heuristic fallback, but the proportion of samples from each source and its effect on learning quality are not analyzed, despite the authors themselves noting this is a 'time–accuracy tradeoff'.

strengths: Well-motivated and practically relevant problem: real-time generation of directional link topologies with parity assignment for mobile ad hoc networks, where combinatorial solvers are too slow and existing heuristics are sub-optimal.

The proposed ACAM tokens are a sensible architectural contribution: detached global tokens with unsoftmaxed cross-attention feeding FiLM modulation give the denoiser access to graph-level statistics (density, sector occupancy), and the ablation (Table 3: CAM vs. ACAM vs. DDPM-GT, saturation 11.62 -> 7.98 -> 7.05) supports the claim that explicit global tokens improve constraint satisfaction.

Partial diffusion for temporal reconfiguration is an elegant use of the diffusion framework (starting the reverse process from the previous topology at a diffusion time proportional to node displacement), and the results (Tables 5-6) show comparable constraint compliance with 3.3-5x fewer steps and improved continuity.

Honest treatment of training-data limitations: the paper explicitly describes the quasi-exhaustive solver with a greedy fallback and discusses the time-accuracy trade-off, and the appendix gives the full greedy algorithm, throughput/interference model, and the topology-correction routine.
Reasonable ablation coverage: loss-term necessity (Table 4, parity 62.23% -> 98.64%), token type, token count, and network-size flexibility (Tables 7-8) are all reported.
weaknesses: Limited reproducibility: the evaluation relies entirely on a proprietary dataset, and the physical simulation parameters are explicitly withheld ('proprietary antenna radiation patterns... out of the scope of this paper'). No code release is mentioned, and the fraction of training samples produced by the greedy fallback is not reported, even though supervision quality depends on it.

Evaluation rigor is thin for a main-track paper: experiments appear to use a single fixed seed (123), several metrics show only small differences (e.g., saturation 12.9% CAM vs. 12.1% ACAM), and variance across seeds is not reported. Some results are relegated to unverifiable prose ('additional experiments not displayed for clarity').

Baselines are comparatively weak or hard to contextualize: GraphVAE (2018) is a dated comparison, and the main diffusion baseline is a re-derived 'DDPM-GT' rather than DiGress itself. TopoFormer, acknowledged as tackling 'a similar problem to ours', is not compared even in an adapted form.

The central claim about ACAM's ability to 'count' is asserted heuristically: no controlled experiment (e.g., synthetic graphs where global cardinalities must be tracked) or analysis isolates why removing softmax yields absolute/counting behavior. The advantage over DiGress-style statistical FiLM features is only anecdotally claimed to grow with capacity.

Novelty is moderate: ACAM tokens are a close variant of virtual nodes/attention registers (Darcet et al., 2023) combined with FiLM conditioning, and partial diffusion closely follows SDEdit-style init-from-partial-noise; the contribution is a well-executed domain-specific combination rather than a new capability.

Scalability is limited and under-discussed in the main text: thorough evaluation is on 16-node graphs, 32-node performance degrades (saturation 14.40% vs. 9.91% target), and networks of 40+ nodes are declared out of scope only in the appendix. The 'constant inference time' claim is not substantiated with a runtime comparison against the combinatorial/heuristic baselines.

Several technical details are imprecise: Eq. 5's noise schedule is unclear (the roles of s and epsilon are not defined precisely), the relation between the BCE losses in Eq. 3 and the discrete state-transition formulation is glossed over, and the extent to which the post-processing correction algorithm (Alg. 2) affects reported metrics (only throughput is explicitly excluded) is ambiguous.
